stem: A 45-year-old woman had documented hepatitis B infection 12 years ago and recovered without antiviral treatment. She is now asymptomatic, and hepatitis B surface antigen is undetectable. Which of the following antibody combinations most strongly supports immunity after natural infection rather than vaccination alone?

options.label: A
options.misconception: Correctly combines surface antibody with evidence of prior core exposure.
options.explanation: Recovery from natural infection commonly leaves both antibody to the surface antigen and antibody to the core antigen. Core antibody distinguishes this history from vaccination alone.

options.label: B
options.misconception: Chooses the pattern of vaccine-only immunity.
options.explanation: Surface antibody without core antibody is expected after vaccination but does not document previous natural infection.

options.label: C
options.misconception: Recognizes prior core exposure but omits the surface antibody expected after recovery.
options.explanation: Core antibody alone does not provide the typical combined antibody pattern described after recovery from natural hepatitis B infection.

options.label: D
options.misconception: Selects a pattern with no serologic evidence of immunity or prior infection.
options.explanation: The absence of both antibodies would not support either recovered natural infection or a successful vaccine response.

options.label: E
options.misconception: Uses an antigen linked to infectivity while omitting evidence of core exposure.
options.explanation: Hepatitis B e antigen does not establish the expected antibody pattern of remote, resolved natural infection.

context:
Learning objective: Differentiate resolved natural hepatitis B infection from vaccine-only immunity using core antibody.

Natural infection exposes the immune system to both surface and core antigens. After recovery, anti-HBs and anti-HBc are typically both detectable; vaccination alone produces anti-HBs without anti-HBc.
